number_of_offences: Charged with multiple offences under Sections 420, 468, 471 IPC and Section 12(b) of the Passports Act, 1967; however, the High Court and Trial Magistrate's orders were set aside
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the State FSL report explicitly stated that the alleged forgery of Respondent No. 2’s signatures on the passport application was inconclusive.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that the motivations of the appellants were not rooted in deceit and that the grant of the passport to the minor child did not result in any loss or damage to respondent no. 2.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 02.06.2008 (child's birth), 07.04.2010 (complaint filed), 13.05.2010 (complaint lodged by respondent no. 2), 15.03.2018 (trial magistrate's order), 18.02.2021 (high court's order), 22 January 2024 (supreme court's judgment)
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Ranbir Singh Yadav, Mohammed Sharookh, Prateek Yadav, Ms. Anzu K. Varkey, Ms. Mahesh Sharma, Ms. Chembugari Abheeshna. Counsel for the State: Narendra Hodda, Sr. Adv., Sanchit Garga, R. D. Singh, Ms. Mithu Jain, Kunal Rana, Pranshu Kaushal
investigation_status: Supplementary charge-sheet filed on 25.07.2017, investigation deemed lacking in rigour and failed to satisfy s.173(8) Cr.P.C.
procedural_irregularity: The supplementary chargesheet relied on the Truth Lab report, which was already available when the original chargesheet was filed, and failed to satisfy the requisites of s.173(8) Cr.P.C.

appeal_history.trial_court: Order dated 15.03.2018 declined to discharge the appellants
appeal_history.high_court: Order dated 18.02.2021 dismissed the criminal revision petition
appeal_history.supreme_court: Appeal allowed, impugned judgments set aside

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellants forged the signature of respondent No. 2 on the passport application, thereby constituting the offence of cheating u/s. 420 IPC and forgery u/ss. 468 and 471 IPC. They also alleged a violation of s.12(b) of the Passports Act, 1967, and sought further investigation under s.173(8) Cr.P.C.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the actions of the appellants did not constitute deceit or damage, as the passport was obtained for the minor child's benefit and not at the cost of respondent No. 2. They contended that the State FSL report was inconclusive and that the supplementary chargesheet lacked new evidence, thus violating procedural requirements.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principles that the prosecution must establish fraudulent and dishonest intention for cheating and forgery, and that the supplementary chargesheet must contain fresh evidence to satisfy s.173(8) Cr.P.C.
precedent_relied_upon: Krishna Chawla v. State of UP [2021] 2 SCR 550; Sushil Suri v. Central Bureau of Investigation [2011] 8 SCR 1; Vinay Tyagi v. Irshad Ali and others [2012] 13 SCR 1005; Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India and another [1978] 2 SCR 621; K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India [2018] 8 SCR 1
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court weighed that the grant of the passport to the minor child was not at the cost of any loss or damage to respondent No. 2, and that the motivations of the appellants were not rooted in deceit.
other_sentence_order: Respondent No. 2 is liable to pay the cost of Rs. 1,00,000/- to Appellant No. 1.
